text:
I’m 26, single, and living alone in a mini-flat that costs ₦400,000 a year in Ipaja.

Last year, I interviewed for a Content Lead role in Ikoyi with a salary of ₦300,000 per month. After four rounds of interviews, HR said during the final chat:

“You’re our pick. You can resume on December 4.”

That same week, I resigned from my ₦160,000 job and even bought a new blazer for the role.

Then on December 1, I got a message:

“Hi, we’ve paused hiring till Q2. Apologies.”

Just like that.

No job.

My rent was due on January 2, and I had only ₦62,000 saved.

I kept applying nonstop. Four interviews a week. All virtual. All draining data.

One HR team disappeared after I spent two hours completing their unpaid test project.

Another said:

“You’re great, but we need someone with agency experience.”

The funny thing? The job advert clearly said entry-level.

What broke me wasn’t the money. It was the silence.

I’d wake up every morning, send 10 applications, then sit in my room until nightfall.

My phone became my enemy.

Every notification made my heart jump, then immediately drop when I realised it was just MTN.

I stopped replying to friends because even a simple “What are you doing now?” started to feel like judgment.

Christmas came.

I told everyone I was working from home.

On December 25, I ate Indomie and eggs alone while watching people post family photos and Christmas celebrations online.

I wasn’t hungry. I just felt invisible.

I started doubting everything. Am I not good enough? Do I perform badly in interviews? Am I missing something everyone else can see?

Rejection slowly became part of my daily routine.

Then on January 3, an old freelance client sent me a DM:

“You still write? I need someone. ₦250,000 per month. A colleague of mine also needs your services. I’ve already recommended you, but I wanted to confirm you’re available first.”

No interview.

No assessment.

No five-stage recruitment process.

Just one message.

And just like that, my life started moving again.

Looking back now, job hunting as a single lady in Lagos wasn’t just about rejection emails.

It was calculating whether you could afford to stay safe while broke.

It was wondering how long your savings would last.

It was watching your confidence disappear one rejection at a time.

Nobody sends you a message saying, “You’re still smart” after the twentieth rejection email.

You have to somehow convince yourself to keep going when you’re no longer sure what you’re fighting for.

The biggest lessons?

Never resign because of a verbal offer.

Never leave a job without a signed contract and a clear resumption plan.

Keep building relationships because opportunities often come from people who already know your work.

And please, have an emergency fund.

Even a small one can save you from making desperate decisions when life suddenly changes.

I’m okay now.

But I don’t wish that kind of quiet loneliness on anyone.

What's your toughest job-hunting experience? 

Let's hear it, please 🤲🏾

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
This UK Kitten May Be the First Recorded Cat With No Reproductive Organs

Everyone should meet Beans, the little kitten who has quite literally gone and broken the whole binary. This special one was actually born without any sixual organs at all, meaning it is neither strictly male nor female. Originally named Hope, the tabby-and-white kitten arrived at a Cats Protection centre in Warrington at fifteen weeks old, part of a sadly abandoned litter.

The centre staff had initially all just assumed that the young kitten was female, right up until the vet exam actually happened. It turned out there were simply no external genitals at all to be found on the kitten anywhere. There were also no internal reproductive organs there either, with vets performing careful exploratory checks only to find absolutely nothing at all inside.

Fiona Brockbank, then a senior field veterinary officer with Cats Protection, called the very rare condition sixual organ agenesis. It essentially means the complete failure of those particular organs to properly develop during the early embryonic growth stage. Hermaphrodite cats with both sets are already rare, but a cat with neither was unheard of, and her team found zero documented cases at all.

The very best part of it, though, is that Beans was otherwise a perfectly healthy, playful little kitten. The cat could go about completely normally and remained full of pure energy, so vets soon offered a strong prognosis for a long life. Adoption interest then poured in from across the UK and even distant California, before Beans found a forever home with a student named Jessi Bennett.

15. Science is a means to economics, and the order cannot be reversed. Printing a rocket is science. Producing rockets faster is economics, and it is the point. Great science that is not economic is research, and research is not a venture asset. Put the economics before the science, he says, and you end up understanding neither.

16. Learning is the sourcing strategy. Access is temporary; a good founder will meet ten investors, not one. What survives is understanding the risk better than the other nine. Watch how that compounds: Speciale started in electric vehicles, which taught them storage, which taught them lithium, which sent them to hydrogen for trucks and ships, then to sodium-ion and zinc-air for energy held over time — and now to generation, because nuclear has opened to private companies. “Access is a short-term advantage.”

17. Capital is more intellectual than speculative. On the AI build-out he pushed back on the framing rather than the question. Capital mostly understands what it is doing; it only looks speculative when everyone crowds the same trade and game theory takes over. The risk is not that AI is unproductive. It is that five players spending trillions to win the same race can make a good technology into a bad business. Which is not a technology question at all.

18. Run a different race. He does not want India chasing general intelligence, because arriving second at someone else’s race is a plan to finish second. Build small models that are excellent at one domain: aerospace, defence, automotive, drug discovery. “Why do I need general intelligence? I am the general intelligence. I need specific intelligence.” A model that speeds up drug discovery does not need to be good at poetry.

And the one to leave with. Asked what someone in a completely different field should steal from his, he did not offer a framework. “You just have to assume you don’t know anything and be willing to learn.” Then, unprompted: he is not an engineer. He studied commerce and economics. He has come a long way toward appreciating technology without ever practising it, and thinks the distance is available to anyone who bothers to walk it.

Most retellings reduce the Sirens to beautiful voices that no sailor can resist. Homer gives us something more disturbing. When Odysseus' ship comes within hearing distance, the Sirens do not simply begin singing into the air. They address him directly by name before he has spoken to them: "Odysseus…"

Then they attach two highly charged titles to that name. They call him polyainos, "much praised" or "much sung of" and mega kudos Achaiōn, "great glory of the Achaeans."

Those expressions matter because they point backward toward the world of the Iliad. Polyainos is used of Odysseus in the Iliad and appears only here in the Odyssey. The second title also belongs strongly to the heroic vocabulary of Troy. Scholars have therefore argued that the Sirens are not simply flattering Odysseus. They are summoning an earlier version of him, the celebrated warrior whose fame was made at Troy.

Then they sharpen the temptation. They tell him that they know everything the Greeks and Trojans suffered at Troy and that they know what happens across the earth. Whoever listens, they promise, leaves knowing more than before.

Seen this way, the Sirens do not merely offer beautiful music. They offer Odysseus a song about the world that made him famous. They know his name. They know his war. They know the identity he built there and they promise access to knowledge no ordinary mortal possesses. That may help explain why the scene becomes so psychologically precise.

Odysseus' crew cannot hear any of this because their ears are sealed with wax. Only Odysseus is exposed to the message. When he signals for them to release him, they do not listen to his new command. They follow the one he gave before hearing the song and tighten the ropes instead. 

The mast therefore protects him from more than a beautiful voice. It protects him from a temptation designed around who he already believes himself to be. We cannot prove that Homer imagined the Sirens composing a different song for every passing sailor. The poem never tells us that.

But the one song Homer allows us to hear is unmistakably specific to Odysseus. That makes the Sirens far more interesting than the later image of seductive monsters singing indiscriminately from the rocks. Their weapon is not simply song. It is recognition.

Our Sirens Case File explores this deeper psychological structure and why Odysseus survives in a completely different way from his crew.

Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

Buy links

- Also check Amazon and other retailers for paperback or additional formats as they become available.

About the author
C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She is the author of the popular clean Fiona Quinn Mysteries (cozy mysteries featuring a kindergarten teacher turned sleuth) and the Owl’s Nest Mysteries, as well as children’s books inspired by farm life. In recent years she has added devotionals, including *Harvesting Grace*, as part of her spiritual writing. She is a wife, mom, grandma, dog lover, and self-described helpless chocoholic.

Abstract
As global climate change accelerates, innovative planetary-scale platforms are required to transition from mere mitigation to active ecological restoration. The Pangea-G Platform, anchored by the advanced GURSEN-H EV system, introduces a multi-layered technological framework designed to regulate atmospheric conditions, stabilize global temperatures, and neutralize carbon footprints. This article evaluates the estimated impacts of deploying the GURSEN-H EV system during its first decade and over a 50-year projection period, focusing specifically on climate stabilization, carbon emission reduction, and thermal balance.

1. Introduction
The escalating frequency of extreme weather events, urban heat islands, and rising global temperatures necessitate paradigm shifts in climate engineering and environmental management. The Pangea-G Platform’s GURSEN-H EV infrastructure integrates nano-surface thermal balancing, advanced carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), and atmospheric energy-regulation algorithms. When deployed at scale, this system aims to fundamentally reshape planetary thermodynamics and mitigate anthropogenic climate pressures.

2. Short-Term Projections: The First Decade (Acute Mitigation & System Integration)
During the initial ten years of deployment, the primary objective of the GURSEN-H EV system is to curb acute environmental degradation, stabilize microclimates, and integrate into industrial and urban networks.

Global Carbon Emission Reduction (15% – 25% Decrease):Through continuous hybrid energy harvesting and localized CCUS integration, the system facilitates a cumulative 20% net reduction in global industrial emissions by the end of the 10th year. This rapid deceleration far outpaces conventional decarbonization timelines.
Urban Heat Island Mitigation (30% – 45% Relief):While reversing global temperature curves entirely within a decade is unfeasible, GURSEN-H EV’s nano-surface reflective coatings and thermal-absorption units alleviate urban heat island intensities by approximately 35% in major metropolitan areas, stabilizing microclimatic shifts.

Atmospheric Particulate and Thermal Stabilization:Smart ionization and filtration networks reduce airborne particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) by up to 50%, concurrently balancing localized thermal radiation and preventing localized heat spikes.
3. Long-Term Projections: The 50-Year Horizon (Global Restoration & Permanent Equilibrium)

Over a half-century operational timeline, the GURSEN-H EV system transitions planetary ecosystems from a state of managed decline to a self-sustaining, carbon-negative equilibrium.
Net-Negative Carbon Balance (70% – 90% Reduction / Net Negative):By year 50, the continuous atmospheric scrubbing and inert mineral sequestration capabilities of GURSEN-H EV fully offset residual anthropogenic emissions. The global carbon ledger shifts into a net-negative state, serving as a critical mechanism for returning atmospheric chemistry closer to pre-industrial norms.

Braking Global Temperature Rise (60% – 75% Blockade):Powered by predictive planetary-scale algorithms and high-altitude atmospheric shields, the system disrupts runaway feedback loops. This robust intervention prevents catastrophic mid-century temperature escalation scenarios, keeping global temperature anomalies well below critical tipping points.
Restoration of Hydrological and Thermal Cycles:By optimizing ocean-atmosphere heat transfer and eliminating industrial thermal pollution into water bodies, the system restores natural thermal gradients, safeguarding marine ecosystems and stabilizing precipitation patterns globally.

4. Conclusion
The Pangea-G Platform, driven by the GURSEN-H EV system, offers a transformative pathway for addressing global climate change. By shifting from passive adaptation to active thermal and carbon engineering, the framework provides a scientifically grounded blueprint to achieve long-term climate stability, safeguard atmospheric health, and re-establish a harmonious equilibrium between human industrial activity and planetary boundaries.

The global carbon ledger shifts into a net-negative state, serving as a critical mechanism for returning atmospheric chemistry closer to pre-industrial norms.

Restoration of Hydrological and Thermal Cycles:By optimizing ocean-atmosphere heat transfer and eliminating industrial thermal pollution into water bodies, the system restores natural thermal gradients, safeguarding marine ecosystems and stabilizing precipitation patterns globally.

The Pangea-G Platform, driven by the GURSEN-H EV system, offers a transformative pathway for addressing global climate change. Today is Saragarhi Day.

On 12 September 1897, just 21 Sikh soldiers of the 36th Sikhs, British Indian Army, under Havildar Ishar Singh, defended the isolated signalling post at Saragarhi on the North-West Frontier.

Against them came an estimated 10,000 Afghan/Pashtun tribesmen, principally Afridi and Orakzai, part of the tribal uprising against British rule.

The 21 were offered surrender. They refused. For hours they held the post against repeated assaults, fighting with rifles and finally at close quarters until every defender was dead. All 21 were posthumously awarded the Indian Order of Merit, the highest gallantry decoration then available to Indian soldiers.

Twenty-one Sikhs against roughly 10,000 men.

Saragarhi is one of the great last stands in British military history and a reminder of something too easily forgotten: Sikh soldiers served the British Empire with extraordinary courage and distinction. Their blood is part of our shared history.

Today Britain should remember them.
